column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 19: “Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you”

column2: From ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: I was behind the Prophet ﷺ and he said:

“Young man, I will teach you some words: Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you. Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him before you. When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah. Know that if the whole nation gathered together to benefit you with something,

they would benefit you only with something Allah has already written for you; and if they gathered together to harm you with something, they would harm you only with something Allah has already written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried.”
Al-Tirmidhī reported it and said: “A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.”

In a narration other than al-Tirmidhī's: “Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him in front of you. Make yourself known to Allah in times of ease and He will know you in times of hardship. Know that what missed you was never going to befall you,
and what befell you was never going to miss you. And know that victory comes with patience, relief comes with distress, and with hardship comes ease.”

Al-Tirmidhī recorded this hadith through the narration of Ḥanash al-Ṣanʿānī from Ibn ʿAbbās. Imam Aḥmad also recorded it from the hadith of Ḥanash, together with two other chains that are broken (munqaṭiʿ), without distinguishing the wording of one from another.
The wording of his narration is: “Young man (or: little lad), shall I not teach you some words through which Allah will benefit you?”

I said: Certainly. He said: “Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you. Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him in front of you. Make yourself known to Allah in times of ease and He will know you in times of hardship. When you ask, ask Allah;
and when you seek help, seek help from Allah. The pen has dried with all that is to be. Were all creation together to want to benefit you with something Allah has not decreed,

they would not be able to do it; and were they to want to harm you with something Allah has not written against you, they would not be able to do it. Know that there is much good in patiently enduring what you dislike, that victory comes with patience, that relief comes with distress, and that with hardship comes ease.”

This wording is fuller than the one the Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) cited and attributed to a source other than al-Tirmidhī. The wording the Shaykh cited was reported by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd in his Musnad, with a weak chain, from ʿAṭāʾ,
from Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ likewise attributed it to ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and others in al-Aḥādīth al-Kulliyyah, the work on which the Shaykh's Forty (may Allah have mercy on him) is based.

This hadith has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās by many routes, through a group of narrators that includes his son ʿAlī, his freed slave ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdillāh, ʿUmar the freed slave of Ghufrah, Ibn Abī Mulaykah and others.
The soundest of all its routes is that of Ḥanash al-Ṣanʿānī, which al-Tirmidhī recorded; so said Ibn Mandah and others.

It has also been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ gave Ibn ʿAbbās this counsel in the hadiths of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, Sahl ibn Saʿd and ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaʿfar, but all their chains contain weakness.
Al-ʿUqaylī mentioned that the chains of this hadith are all soft (layyin), some being better than others. In any case, the route of Ḥanash recorded by al-Tirmidhī is good and sound.

This hadith contains great pieces of counsel and universal principles that belong to the most important matters of the religion — so much so that one scholar said: I reflected on this hadith and it overwhelmed me, until I almost lost my senses. What a pity that people are ignorant of this hadith and understand so little of its meaning!
I say: I have devoted a large treatise to its commentary; here we shall set out its main purposes briefly, if Allah the Exalted wills.

His words ﷺ, “Be mindful of Allah” — literally, “guard Allah” — mean: guard His limits, His rights, His commands and His prohibitions. Guarding these means stopping at His commands by carrying them out, at His prohibitions by avoiding them, and at His limits, so as not to go beyond what He has commanded

and permitted into what He has forbidden. Whoever does that is among those who guard the limits of Allah, whom Allah praised in His Book, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: “This is what you were promised — for everyone who constantly turned back [to Allah] and kept [His bounds] (ḥafīẓ), who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart turned to Him in repentance” [Qāf 50:32–33].
Ḥafīẓ here has been explained as one who keeps Allah's commands, and as one who keeps his sins in mind so as to repent of them.

Among the greatest of Allah's commands that must be guarded is the prayer. Allah commanded that it be guarded, saying: “Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer” [al-Baqarah 2:238], and He praised those who guard it, saying: “And those who guard their prayer” [al-Maʿārij 70:34].

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever guards it has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise.” And in another hadith: “Whoever guards them, they will be a light, a proof and a salvation for him on the Day of Resurrection.”
Likewise purification, for it is the key to prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said: “None guards his wuḍūʾ except a believer.”

Among the things one is commanded to guard are oaths. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And guard your oaths” [al-Māʾidah 5:89]. People fall into swearing oaths a great deal, and many of them neglect what their oaths require of them, neither guarding it nor holding to it.

Another is guarding the head and the belly, as in the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd traced back to the Prophet ﷺ (marfūʿ): “Being shy of Allah as He truly deserves is to guard the head and what it holds, and to guard the belly and what it contains.” Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded it.

Guarding the head and what it holds includes guarding the hearing, the sight and the tongue from what is unlawful; and guarding the belly and what it contains includes guarding the heart against persisting in anything unlawful.
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him” [al-Baqarah 2:235]. Allah has gathered all of this in His words: “Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart — about each of these one will be questioned” [al-Isrāʾ 17:36].
It also includes guarding the belly from taking in unlawful food and drink.

Among the greatest things that must be guarded against what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden are the tongue and the private parts. In the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever guards what is between his jaws and what is between his legs will enter Paradise.” Al-Ḥākim recorded it.
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Mūsā, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever guards what is between his jawbones and his private parts will enter Paradise.”

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded that the private parts be guarded and praised those who guard them. He said: “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts” [al-Nūr 24:30]; and: “men who guard their private parts and women who do so, men who remember Allah much and women who do so — for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward” [al-Aḥzāb 33:35];

and: “The believers have indeed succeeded — those who are humble in their prayer” [al-Muʾminūn 23:1–2], up to His words: “and who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not to be blamed” [al-Muʾminūn 23:5–6].
Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī said: The first thing Allah enjoined upon Ādam when He sent him down to earth was to guard his private parts, and He said: Do not place it except in what is lawful.

His words ﷺ, “He will protect you,” mean that whoever guards the limits of Allah and observes His rights, Allah will protect him; for the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. As the Exalted said: “Fulfil My covenant and I will fulfil your covenant” [al-Baqarah 2:40]; “So remember Me; I will remember you” [al-Baqarah 2:152]; and “If you support Allah, He will support you” [Muḥammad 47:7].
Allah's protection of His servant takes in two kinds.

The first is His protecting him in his worldly interests, such as protecting him in his body, his children, his family and his wealth. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “For him there are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who protect him by the command of Allah” [al-Raʿd 13:11].
Ibn ʿAbbās said: They are the angels who protect him by Allah's command; when the decree comes, they leave him.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: With every man there are two angels who protect him from what has not been decreed; when the decree comes, they leave him to it. A man's appointed term is a strong shield.

Mujāhid said: There is no servant but that he has an angel who protects him, asleep and awake, from jinn, humans and vermin. Nothing comes at him but the angel says: Back! — except something Allah has permitted, which then befalls him.

Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never left off these supplications in the evening and in the morning: “O Allah, I ask You for well-being in this world and the Hereafter.

O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion and my worldly life, my family and my wealth. O Allah, cover my faults and calm my fears. Guard me from before me and from behind me, from my right and from my left, and from above me; and I seek refuge in Your greatness from being taken unawares from beneath me.”
Whoever is mindful of Allah in his youth and strength, Allah will protect him in his old age and frailty, and let him enjoy his hearing, his sight, his ability, his strength and his mind.

One scholar had passed a hundred years of age while still enjoying his strength and his mind. One day he made a mighty leap, and when he was reproached for it he said: These are limbs we guarded from sins in our youth, so Allah has preserved them for us in our old age.
The opposite of this: one of the Salaf saw an old man begging from people and said: This man neglected Allah in his youth, so Allah has neglected him in his old age.

Allah may also protect a servant, after his death, in his descendants because of his righteousness, as has been said concerning the words of the Exalted, “And their father had been righteous” [al-Kahf 18:82]: that the two boys were protected because of their father's righteousness.

Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib said to his son: I shall add to my prayer for your sake, in the hope that I will be protected in you. Then he recited this verse: “And their father had been righteous.” ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: No believer dies but that Allah protects him in his offspring and his offspring's offspring.
Ibn al-Munkadir said: Through a righteous man Allah protects his children, his children's children and the little houses around him, and they remain under Allah's protection and covering.

Whenever the servant is occupied with obeying Allah, Allah protects him in that state. In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There was a woman in a house, and she went out with a raiding party of the Muslims,

leaving behind twelve she-goats and her ṣīṣiyah, with which she used to weave.” He said: “She lost one of her goats and her ṣīṣiyah, and she said: My Lord, You have guaranteed to whoever goes out in Your path that You will guard what he leaves behind. I have lost a goat from my flock and my ṣīṣiyah, and I implore You for my goat and my ṣīṣiyah.”
The narrator said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ began describing how earnestly she implored her Lord, Blessed and Exalted is He. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“And in the morning she had her goat and another like it, and her ṣīṣiyah and another like it.”
The ṣīṣiyah is the hook with which yarn is spun and woven.
So whoever is mindful of Allah, Allah protects him from every harm.
One of the Salaf said: Whoever fears Allah has protected himself, and whoever neglects his taqwā has lost himself — and Allah has no need of him.

Among the wonders of Allah's protection of whoever is mindful of Him is that He makes animals that are harmful by nature guard him from harm. So it happened to Safīnah, the freed slave of the Prophet ﷺ, when the ship he was on was wrecked

and he came ashore on an island. He saw a lion, which began walking with him until it led him to the road. When it had brought him to the road, it began to growl softly, as though bidding him farewell, and then went back.
Ibrāhīm ibn Adham was seen asleep in a garden with a snake beside him holding a sprig of narcissus in its mouth, and it kept warding things off him until he woke.

The opposite of this is that whoever neglects Allah, Allah neglects him, and he is lost among His creation, until harm and injury reach him even from those he hoped would benefit him, his family and others. As one of the Salaf said: When I disobey Allah, I can see it in the behaviour of my servant and my riding animal.

The second kind of protection — and it is the nobler of the two — is Allah's protecting His servant in his religion and his faith. He protects him during his life from misleading doubts and unlawful desires, and protects his religion for him at his death, so that He takes him in a state of faith. One of the Salaf said:

When a man is at the point of death, the angel is told: Smell his head. It says: I find the Qurʾān in his head. It is told: Smell his heart. It says: I find fasting in his heart. It is told: Smell his feet. It says: I find standing in prayer in his feet. Then it is said: He guarded himself, so Allah has guarded him.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib relates that the Prophet ﷺ told him to say on going to sleep: If You take my soul, have mercy on it; and if You release it, protect it with that by which You protect Your righteous servants.

In the hadith of ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ taught him to say: O Allah, protect me through Islam when standing, protect me through Islam when sitting, protect me through Islam when lying down, and do not let any enemy or envier have their way with me.
Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

When someone intended to travel, the Prophet ﷺ would bid him farewell, saying: “I entrust to Allah your religion, your trust and the final outcomes of your deeds.” And he used to say: “When something is entrusted to Allah, He protects it.”
Al-Nasāʾī and others recorded it.
In sum, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, protects the religion of the believer who guards His limits, and comes between him and whatever would corrupt his religion through various kinds of protection,

some of which the servant may not even perceive, and some of which he may dislike. As He said concerning Yūsuf (peace be upon him): “Thus it was, so that We might avert from him evil and indecency; indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants” [Yūsuf 12:24].
Ibn ʿAbbās said concerning the words of the Exalted, “that Allah comes between a man and his heart” [al-Anfāl 8:24]: He comes between the believer and the sin that would drag him to the Fire.
Al-Ḥasan said, speaking of those who commit sins: They were worthless to Him, so they disobeyed Him; had they been dear to Him, He would have kept them from sin.
Ibn Masʿūd said: A servant sets his heart on some matter of trade or authority until it is about to be made easy for him. Then Allah looks at him and says to the angels: Turn it away from him,

for if I make it easy for him I will admit him to the Fire. So Allah turns it away from him, and he goes on blaming his ill luck, saying: So-and-so beat me to it, so-and-so outwitted me — when it was nothing but the grace of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded something of this, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: Among My servants are some whose faith is set right only by poverty;
were I to give him plenty, that would corrupt him. Among My servants are some whose faith is set right only by wealth; were I to make him poor, that would corrupt him.

Among My servants are some whose faith is set right only by health; were I to make him ill, that would corrupt him. Among My servants are some whose faith is set right only by illness; were I to make him healthy,

that would corrupt him. Among My servants are some who seek a certain door of worship, and I hold him back from it so that self-admiration does not enter him. I direct the affairs of My servants by My knowledge of what is in their hearts; I am All-Knowing, All-Aware.”
His words ﷺ, “Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him before you” — in one narration, “in front of you” — mean that whoever guards the limits of Allah and observes His rights

will find Allah with him in all his states, wherever he turns, surrounding him, helping him, protecting him, granting him success and keeping him on the right course; for “Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good” [al-Naḥl 16:128]. Qatādah said:
Whoever fears Allah, Allah is with him; and whoever has Allah with him has with him the party that is never defeated, the guard who never sleeps, and the guide who never goes astray.
One of the Salaf wrote to a brother of his: To proceed: if Allah is with you, whom do you fear?
And if He is against you, in whom do you hope?

This special companionship (maʿiyyah) is the one mentioned in the words of the Exalted to Mūsā and Hārūn: “Do not fear; I am with you both, hearing and seeing” [Ṭā Hā 20:46]; in the words of Mūsā: “Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me” [al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:62];
and in the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Abū Bakr when the two of them were in the cave: “What do you think of two whose third is Allah?
Do not grieve; Allah is with us.”
This special companionship entails help and support, protection and aid — unlike the general companionship mentioned in the words of the Exalted:
“There is no private conversation of three but He is their fourth, nor of five but He is their sixth, nor of fewer than that or more but He is with them wherever they are” [al-Mujādilah 58:7];
and in His words: “They do not hide from Allah, and He is with them when they spend the night plotting words He does not approve” [al-Nisāʾ 4:108].

This companionship entails His knowledge of their deeds, His seeing them and His watching over them, and so it calls for His servants to fear Him; whereas the first companionship entails protecting, guarding and helping the servant. So whoever is mindful of Allah and observes His rights

will find Him before him and in front of him in every situation; he will find comfort in Him and, through Him, have no need of His creation — as in the hadith, “The best faith is that the servant knows that Allah is with him wherever he is,” which has already been cited.
It is narrated of Bunān al-Ḥammāl that he went into the desert alone on the road to Tabūk and felt lonely, and a voice called out to him: Why do you feel lonely?
Is your Beloved not with you?
Someone was asked: Do you not feel lonely on your own?
He said: How could I feel lonely when He says:
“I sit with whoever remembers Me”? Another was told: We see you alone.
He said: How can someone who has Allah with him be alone? Another was asked: Have you no companion to keep you company?
He said: Yes. He was asked: Where is he?
He said: In front of me, behind me, on my right, on my left and above me.
Al-Shiblī used to recite:
When we travel by night with You before us, / the remembrance of You is guide enough for our mounts.

His words ﷺ, “Make yourself known to Allah in times of ease and He will know you in times of hardship,” mean that when the servant fears Allah, guards His limits and observes His rights in his time of ease, he has thereby made himself known to Allah,

and a special acquaintance has formed between him and his Lord. So his Lord knows him in hardship and honours for him the way he made himself known to Him in ease, and rescues him from hardships through this acquaintance. This is a special knowing that entails the servant's nearness to his Lord, His love for him and His answering his supplication.
The servant's knowledge of his Lord is of two kinds.
The first is general knowledge: the knowledge of acknowledging Him, affirming His truth and believing in Him. This is shared by all believers.

The second is a special knowledge that entails the heart's turning wholly towards Allah, devoting itself to Him alone, finding intimacy with Him, being at rest in His remembrance, feeling shy before Him and holding Him in awe.

It is around this special knowledge that the knowers of Allah revolve, as one of them said: Poor are the people of this world! They left it without tasting the sweetest thing in it. He was asked: And what is that?
He said: Knowing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Aḥmad ibn ʿĀṣim al-Anṭākī said: I would like not to die until I know my Master — and knowing Him is not merely acknowledging Him, but the knowledge that, once you know Him, makes you shy before Him.
Allah's knowledge of His servant is likewise of two kinds.

General knowledge, which is His knowledge, Glorified is He, of His servants, and His awareness of what they conceal and what they disclose, as He said: “We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him” [Qāf 50:16]; and: “He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and since you were foetuses in your mothers' wombs” [al-Najm 53:32].

The second is special knowledge, which entails His love for His servant, drawing him near, answering his supplication and rescuing him from hardships. This is what the Prophet ﷺ pointed to in what he relates from his Lord: “My servant keeps drawing near to Me with voluntary deeds until I love him;

and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks refuge with Me, I will surely grant him refuge.” In one narration: “And if he calls on Me, I will surely answer him.”
When al-Ḥasan fled from al-Ḥajjāj, he went into the house of Ḥabīb Abū Muḥammad, and Ḥabīb said to him:
Abū Saʿīd, is there not something between you and your Lord by which you can call on Him, so that He hides you from these people?

Go into the house. He went in, and the guards came in after him but did not see him. When this was mentioned to al-Ḥajjāj, he said: No, he was in the house, but Allah blotted out their sight so that they did not see him.

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ met Shaʿwānah, the devout worshipper, and asked her to pray for him. She said: Fuḍayl, is there nothing between you and Him such that, if you called on Him, He would answer you? And al-Fuḍayl fainted.
Maʿrūf was asked what had stirred him to devote himself wholly to worship — the questioner mentioning death, the barzakh, Paradise and the Fire.
Maʿrūf said: A King in whose hand all this lies — if there is acquaintance between you and Him, He will suffice you against all of it.
In sum, whoever deals with Allah through taqwā and obedience in his time of ease, Allah will deal with him through gentleness and help in his time of hardship.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever would be glad for Allah to answer him in times of hardship, let him supplicate much in times of ease.”
Ibn Abī Ḥātim and others recorded, through the narration of Yazīd al-Raqāshī from Anas, tracing it back to the Prophet ﷺ, that when Yūnus (peace be upon him) supplicated in the belly of the whale,
the angels said: Lord, this is a familiar voice from a strange land. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: Do you not recognise it?
They said: Who is it?
He said: My servant Yūnus. They said: Your servant Yūnus, for whom accepted deeds and answered supplications never ceased to be raised up?
He said: Yes. They said: Lord, will You not have mercy on him for what he used to do in times of ease, and rescue him from this affliction?
He said: Certainly. The narrator said:
So Allah commanded the whale, and it cast him out onto the bare shore.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays said: Remember Allah in times of ease and He will remember you in times of hardship. Yūnus (peace be upon him) used to remember Allah the Exalted, and when he fell into the belly of the whale, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“Had he not been of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected” [al-Ṣāffāt 37:143–144]. Pharaoh, by contrast, was a tyrant, forgetful of the remembrance of Allah; when drowning overtook him, he said: I believe. And Allah the Exalted said: “Now? When you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters!” [Yūnus 10:91].

Salmān al-Fārisī said: When a man is one who supplicates much in good times, and then adversity befalls him and he calls on Allah the Exalted, the angels say: A familiar voice — and they intercede for him.
But when he is not one who supplicates much in good times, and adversity befalls him and he calls on Allah the Exalted, the angels say: An unfamiliar voice — and they do not intercede for him.
A man said to Abū al-Dardāʾ: Give me some counsel. He said: Remember Allah in good times, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will remember you in adversity.
It is also related from him that he said: Call on Allah on the day of your good fortune; perhaps He will answer you on the day of your adversity.

The greatest hardship to befall the servant in this world is death, and what comes after it is harder still, unless the servant's destination is a good one. So the believer must prepare for death and what follows it, while he is in health, through taqwā and righteous deeds.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “O you who believe, fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow; and fear Allah — indeed, Allah is aware of what you do. And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves; it is they who are the defiantly disobedient” [al-Ḥashr 59:18–19].

Whoever remembers Allah in his health and ease, and prepares then to meet Allah through death and what lies after it, Allah will remember him in these hardships: He will be with him in them, be gentle with him,

help him, take charge of him and keep him firm upon tawḥīd, so that he meets Him while He is pleased with him. And whoever forgets Allah in his health and ease, and does not then prepare to meet Him, Allah will forget him in these hardships,

meaning that He will turn away from him and leave him to himself. When death comes to the believer who has prepared for it, he thinks well of his Lord, glad tidings come to him from Allah, and he loves to meet Allah, and Allah loves to meet him.

The wicked man is the reverse of this. At that point the believer rejoices and is glad at what he has sent ahead, to which he is now going, while the negligent one is filled with regret and says: “Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah!” [al-Zumar 39:56].
Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī said before his death: How could I not have hope in my Lord, when I have fasted eighty Ramaḍāns for Him?
Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said to his son at his death: Do you think Allah will let go to waste forty years in which your father completed the Qurʾān every night?
Ādam ibn Abī Iyās completed the Qurʾān while lying covered for death, and then said: By my love for You, will You not be gentle with me as I lie dying?
I was hoping in You for this day; I used to hope in You. There is no god but Allah. Then he passed away.
When Zakariyyā ibn ʿAdī was dying, he raised his hands and said: O Allah, I long for You.
ʿAbd al-Ṣamad the ascetic said at his death: My Master, for this hour I stored You up, and for this day I kept You. Make my good opinion of You come true.
Qatādah said concerning the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, “And whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2]: Out of the distress of death.
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning this verse: He will rescue him from every distress in this world and the Hereafter.

Zayd ibn Aslam said concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic, “Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast — the angels descend upon them, [saying,] ‘Do not fear and do not grieve’” [Fuṣṣilat 41:30], to the end of the verse:
He is given these glad tidings at his death, in his grave and on the day he is resurrected, so that he is in Paradise while the joy of the glad tidings has still not left his heart.

Thābit al-Bunānī said concerning this verse: It has reached us that when Allah raises the believer from his grave, the two angels who were with him in this world meet him and say to him: Do not fear and do not grieve.

So Allah calms his fear and makes his eye cool with delight. There is no terror that overwhelms people on the Day of Resurrection but it is, for the believer, a delight to the eye, because Allah guided him and because of what he used to do in this world.

His words ﷺ, “When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah,” are drawn from the words of the Exalted: “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help” [al-Fātiḥah 1:5]. Asking of Allah is calling on Him and turning to Him in desire, and supplication is worship;

so it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, after which he recited the words of the Exalted: “And your Lord said: Call on Me; I will answer you” [Ghāfir 40:60]. Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded it.

Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Supplication is the marrow of worship.” These words, then, include asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and not asking anyone else, and seeking help from Allah to the exclusion of anyone else.
As for asking: Allah has commanded us to ask Him, saying: “And ask Allah of His bounty” [al-Nisāʾ 4:32].
Al-Tirmidhī's collection has, from Ibn Masʿūd, as marfūʿ:
“Ask Allah of His bounty, for Allah loves to be asked.”
It also has, from Abū Hurayrah, as marfūʿ: “Whoever does not ask Allah, He is angry with him.”
In another hadith: “Let each of you ask his Lord for all his needs — even for the strap of his sandal when it breaks.”
There are many authentic hadiths forbidding asking created beings. The Prophet ﷺ took the pledge of a number of his Companions that they would not ask people for anything,
among them Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, Abū Dharr and Thawbān. If one of them dropped his whip or his camel's halter, he would not ask anyone to hand it to him.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded, from the hadith of Abū ʿUbaydah ibn ʿAbdillāh ibn Masʿūd, that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Messenger of Allah, the clan of So-and-so raided me and took my son and my camels.

The Prophet ﷺ said to him: “The family of Muḥammad are such-and-such a number of households, and they have not a mudd or a ṣāʿ of food between them. So ask Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” He went back to his wife, who said: What did he say to you?
He told her, and she said: What an excellent reply he gave you! Before long Allah returned his son and his camels to him, more plentiful than they had been. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him,

and the Prophet ascended the minbar, praised and extolled Allah, commanded the people to ask of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to turn to Him in desire, and recited: “And whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2–3].
It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “Is there anyone calling on Me, that I may answer him?
Is there anyone asking of Me, that I may give him?
Is there anyone seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?”
Al-Maḥāmilī and others recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah the Exalted said: Who is it that called on Me and I did not answer him,
asked of Me and I did not give him,
sought My forgiveness and I did not forgive him,
when I am the Most Merciful of those who show mercy?”
Know that asking Allah the Exalted, and not His creation, is what is required;

for asking involves the asker displaying his abasement, his lowliness, his need and his want, and acknowledging that the one asked is able to remove this harm, grant what is sought, bring benefit and ward off injury. Abasement and want befit none but Allah alone,

because they are the very reality of worship. Imam Aḥmad used to supplicate, saying: O Allah, as You have kept my face from prostrating to anyone but You, keep it from asking anyone but You. And none but He is able to remove harm and bring benefit,

as He said: “And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none who can remove it but He; and if He intends good for you, there is none who can repel His bounty” [Yūnus 10:107]; and: “Whatever mercy Allah opens to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him” [Fāṭir 35:2].

Allah, Glorified is He, loves to be asked, to have people turn to Him in desire for their needs, and to be implored insistently in asking and supplication. He is angry with whoever does not ask Him, and He calls on His servants to ask Him.

He is able to give all His creation what they ask without anything being diminished from His dominion. The created being is the opposite in all of this: he dislikes being asked and would rather not be asked, because of his incapacity, his poverty and his need.

This is why Wahb ibn Munabbih said to a man who used to frequent kings: Woe to you! You go to one who shuts his door on you, shows you his poverty and hides his riches from you, and you leave the One who opens His door to you in the middle of the night and the middle of the day, shows you His riches, and says: Call on Me and I will answer you?!

Ṭāwūs said to ʿAṭāʾ: Beware of seeking your needs from one who has shut his door against you and set his chamberlain in front of them. Keep to the One whose door is open until the Day of Resurrection, who has commanded you to ask Him and promised to answer you.
As for seeking help from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, rather than from any other created being:

that is because the servant cannot, by himself alone, secure his interests and ward off what harms him, and he has no helper in the interests of his religion and his worldly life except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever Allah helps is truly helped, and whoever He forsakes is truly forsaken. This is the true meaning of the words:

“There is no might and no power except through Allah” (lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh). Its meaning is: the servant has no turning from one state to another, and no power to do so, except through Allah. It is a mighty phrase, one of the treasures of Paradise. The servant needs to seek Allah's help in doing what is commanded,

leaving what is forbidden, and patiently bearing all that is decreed, in this world, at death and after it, through the terrors of the barzakh and the Day of Resurrection; and none can help him in that except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever truly seeks His help in all of that, He will help him.
In the authentic hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Be keen on what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up.”
Whoever abandons seeking help from Allah and seeks help from another, Allah leaves him to the one whose help he sought, and he ends up forsaken.
Al-Ḥasan wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: Do not seek help from anyone but Allah, or Allah will leave you to him.
Among the sayings of one of the Salaf: My Lord, I marvel at one who knows You — how can he hope in anyone else? I marvel at one who knows You — how can he seek help from anyone else?

His words ﷺ, “The pen has dried with all that is to be” — and in another narration, “The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried” — are a figure of speech for the writing of all the decrees having been done beforehand and finished long ago. For when the writing of a book has been completed,

the pens have been lifted from it and a long time has passed, then the pens have indeed been lifted from it, the pens it was written with have dried of their ink, and the page it was written on has dried of the ink written on it. This is one of the finest and most eloquent of figures.
The Book and many authentic hadiths point to the same meaning. Allah the Exalted said:
“No calamity befalls on the earth or in yourselves but it is in a record before We bring it into being; indeed, that is easy for Allah” [al-Ḥadīd 57:22].
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah wrote down the decrees of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.”
It also has, from Jābir, that a man said: Messenger of Allah, what do our deeds today rest upon?
Upon what the pens have dried with and the decrees have run with, or upon something still to come?
He said: “No — upon what the pens have dried with and the decrees have run with.” The man said: Then what are deeds for?
He said: “Act, for everyone is eased towards what he was created for.”

Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The first thing Allah created was the pen. Then He said: Write. And in that very hour it ran with all that is to be until the Day of Resurrection.”
The hadiths with this meaning are very many; it would take too long to mention them.

His words ﷺ: “Were all creation together to want to benefit you with something Allah has not decreed, they would not be able to do it; and were they to want to harm you with something Allah has not written against you, they would not be able to do it.”
This is the narration of Imam Aḥmad, and al-Tirmidhī's narration has the same meaning. What is meant is that whatever befalls the servant in his worldly life, harmful or beneficial,
has all been decreed for him, and nothing befalls the servant except what was written for him of it in the prior record, even if all creation together strove [to make it otherwise].
The Qurʾān points to the like of this in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: “Say: Nothing will befall us except what Allah has written for us” [al-Tawbah 9:51]; and His words:

“No calamity befalls on the earth or in yourselves but it is in a record before We bring it into being” [al-Ḥadīd 57:22]; and His words: “Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those for whom killing was written would have gone out to the places where they were to lie” [Āl ʿImrān 3:154].

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Everything has a reality, and no servant attains the reality of faith until he knows that what befell him was never going to miss him, and what missed him was never going to befall him.”
Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah recorded the same meaning from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thābit, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Know that this whole counsel revolves around this principle; whatever is mentioned before it and after it branches off from it and goes back to it.

For when the servant knows that nothing will befall him except what Allah has written for him — good or evil, benefit or harm — and that all creation striving against what has been decreed is of no use whatsoever,

he then knows that Allah alone is the One who harms and benefits, who gives and withholds. That obliges the servant to affirm the oneness of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, to single Him out with obedience and to guard His limits; for what is sought in worshipping anything is only to bring benefit and ward off harm.
That is why Allah condemned those who worship what neither benefits nor harms and avails its worshipper nothing. Whoever knows that none benefits or harms,
gives or withholds, except Allah, is obliged by that to single Him out with fear, hope, love, asking, humble entreaty and supplication; to put obedience to Him before obedience to all creation;

to guard against His displeasure even if it means the displeasure of all creation; to single Him out in seeking help and in asking; and to make supplication sincerely to Him in times of hardship and of ease —
unlike the idolaters, who would call on Him sincerely in hardships, forget Him in ease, and call on those besides Him from whom they hoped for benefit. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“Say: Have you considered what you call on besides Allah? If Allah intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy? Say: Allah is sufficient for me; upon Him let all who rely place their reliance” [al-Zumar 39:38].

His words ﷺ, “Know that there is much good in patiently enduring what you dislike,” mean that when the servant is patient with the painful calamities written for him that befall him, there is much good for him in that patience.

In the narration of ʿUmar the freed slave of Ghufrah and others from Ibn ʿAbbās there is a further addition before these words: “If you are able to act for Allah with contentment in certainty, then do so; and if you are not able, then there is much good in patiently enduring what you dislike.”
In another narration — that of ʿAlī ibn ʿAbdillāh ibn ʿAbbās from his father,
though its chain is weak — there is a further addition after this: I said: Messenger of Allah, how am I to attain certainty?
He said: “By knowing that what befell you was never going to miss you, and what missed you was never going to befall you; then you will have mastered the door of certainty.”
The meaning of this is that when the heart attains certainty about the prior decree and the destiny already settled, this helps the servant's soul to be content with what has befallen it.

So whoever is able, through certainty in the decree and destiny, to act with contentment at what has been decreed, let him do so; and if he is unable to be content, then there is much good in patiently enduring what is disliked.
These, then, are two degrees for the believer in the decree and destiny when calamities strike.

The first is to be content with it, and this is a lofty degree, very high indeed. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “No calamity strikes except by Allah's permission, and whoever believes in Allah, He will guide his heart” [al-Taghābun 64:11].
ʿAlqamah said: It is the calamity that strikes a man, and he knows it is from Allah, so he submits to it and is content.
Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When Allah loves a people, He tests them;

whoever is content will have [His] good pleasure, and whoever is resentful will have [His] displeasure.” And the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “I ask You for contentment after the decree.”

Among the things that lead the believer to contentment with the decree is realising in his faith the meaning of the Prophet's words ﷺ: “Allah decrees nothing for the believer but that it is good for him:
if good fortune befalls him he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if adversity befalls him he is patient, and that is good for him. And that is for none but the believer.”
A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him for a comprehensive, concise piece of counsel, and he said: “Do not suspect Allah in His decree.”
Abū al-Dardāʾ said: When Allah decrees something, He loves that it be accepted with contentment. Ibn Masʿūd said: Allah, by His equity and justice, placed relief and joy in certainty and contentment,

and placed worry and grief in doubt and resentment. So the one who is content wishes for nothing other than the state he is in, whether hardship or ease. This has been narrated from ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd and others.
ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: I have come to have no joy except where the decree and destiny fall.
Whoever reaches this degree spends his whole life in bliss and joy. Allah the Exalted said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while being a believer — We will surely give him a good life” [al-Naḥl 16:97]. One of the Salaf said: The good life is contentment and being satisfied with little.
ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Zayd said: Contentment is Allah's greatest door, the paradise of this world, and the resting place of the worshippers.

The people of contentment sometimes keep in view the wisdom of the One who tests them and His choosing what is best for His servant in the trial, and that He is not to be suspected in His decree. Sometimes they keep in view the reward for contentment with the decree, and it makes them forget the pain of what was decreed. And sometimes they keep in view the greatness, majesty and perfection of the One who tests them,

and become so absorbed in contemplating that that they no longer feel the pain. This is attained by the elect among the people of knowledge [of Allah] and love, so that they may even take delight in what befalls them, because they see that it comes from their Beloved — as one of them said: He let them find sweetness (ʿudhūbah) in His torment (ʿadhāb).
One of the Successors was asked how he was during his illness, and he said: What is most beloved to Him is most beloved to me.
Al-Sarī was asked: Does the lover feel the pain of affliction? He said: No. And someone said:
[Love's] torment for Your sake is sweet, / and its distance for Your sake is nearness.
You are to me as my own soul — / no, You are dearer to me than it.
It is enough for me of love / that I love whatever You love.

The second degree is to be patient with the affliction, and this is for one who cannot attain contentment with the decree. Contentment is a virtue that is encouraged and recommended, whereas patience is binding on the believer, an obligation. There is much good in patience, for Allah has commanded it and promised an abundant reward for it.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Only the patient will be given their reward in full, without measure” [al-Zumar 39:10]; and: “Give glad tidings to the patient, who, when a calamity strikes them, say: ‘We belong to Allah, and to Him we shall return.’ Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and it is they who are rightly guided” [al-Baqarah 2:155–157].
Al-Ḥasan said: Contentment is rare, but patience is the believer's mainstay.

The difference between contentment and patience is this. Patience is restraining and holding back the soul from resentment while the pain is felt and one wishes it gone, and restraining the limbs from acting as anguish would dictate. Contentment is the heart's openness and ease with the decree,

and ceasing to wish that the painful thing be gone, even if the pain is still felt; contentment lightens it, because of the refreshment of certainty and knowledge that touches the heart. When contentment grows strong, it may take away the feeling of pain altogether, as has been mentioned.

His words ﷺ, “Know that victory comes with patience,” agree with the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission! And Allah is with the patient” [al-Baqarah 2:249];

and His words, Exalted is He: “If there are among you a hundred who are patient, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by Allah's permission; and Allah is with the patient” [al-Anfāl 8:66].
ʿUmar said to some elders of Banū ʿAbs: With what did you fight people?
They said: With patience. We never met a people but we held out against them as long as they held out against us.
One of the Salaf said: All of us dislike death and the pain of wounds, but we surpass one another in patience. And al-Baṭṭāl said:
Courage is an hour's patience.

This is in fighting the outward enemy, that is, jihād against the disbelievers. It is the same in fighting the inward enemy, that is, the struggle against the self and its whims; for struggling against these is among the greatest forms of jihād, as the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The mujāhid is the one who strives against his own self for the sake of Allah.”
ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said to someone who asked him about jihād: Begin with yourself and strive against it; begin with yourself and wage war on it.

Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd said: Ibrāhīm ibn Adham informed us, saying: A trustworthy narrator told us, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said: The first part of your jihād that you will come to disown is the struggle against your own selves.
Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAblah said to some people who had come back from a campaign: You have come from the lesser jihād; what have you done in the greater jihād?
They said: What is the greater jihād?
He said: The jihād of the heart.
This is narrated as a marfūʿ hadith of Jābir, with a weak chain, in the wording: “You have come from the lesser jihād to the greater jihād.” They said: What is the greater jihād?
He said: “The servant's struggle against his own whims.”
It is narrated, from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Sinān from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Your enemy is not the one who, if he kills you, admits you to Paradise, and if you kill him, becomes a light for you. Your worst enemy is your own self, between your two sides.”

Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq said in his counsel to ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) when he appointed him as his successor: The first thing I warn you against is your own self, between your two sides.
This jihād, too, requires patience. Whoever patiently struggles against his self, his whims and his devil overcomes them, gains victory and triumph, and becomes master of himself,

and so he becomes mighty, a king. Whoever is impatient and does not patiently struggle against them is overcome, subdued and taken captive, and becomes a lowly slave, a prisoner in the hands of his devil and his whims. As it has been said:
When a man does not overcome his desire, it sets him down / in a place where even the mighty is brought low.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: Whoever is patient — how short a time he has to be patient! And whoever gives way to anguish — how short a time he has to enjoy himself!

So his words ﷺ, “Victory comes with patience,” include victory in both jihāds: the jihād against the outward enemy and the jihād against the inward enemy. Whoever is patient in both is given victory and triumphs over his enemy; whoever is not patient in them but gives way to anguish is subdued, and becomes his enemy's captive or is slain by him.

His words ﷺ, “And relief comes with distress”: this is attested by the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, “It is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy” [al-Shūrā 42:28], and by the words of the Prophet ﷺ:

“Our Lord laughs at the despair of His servants while change is near.” Imam Aḥmad recorded it, and his son ʿAbdullāh recorded it within a long hadith, in which there is: “Allah knows the day of rain; He looks down on you, distressed and despairing, and keeps laughing, knowing that your change is near.”

The meaning is that He, Glorified is He, marvels at His servants' despair when rain is withheld from them, at their despondency and their giving up hope of mercy, when the time of His relief and mercy for His servants — sending down rain on them and changing their state — has drawn near without their realising it.

The Exalted said: “Then when He causes it to fall on whom He wills of His servants, at once they rejoice, though before it was sent down upon them they were in despair” [al-Rūm 30:48–49]. The Exalted said: “Until, when the messengers despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them” [Yūsuf 12:110]. And the Exalted said:
“…until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: When will the help of Allah come? Truly, the help of Allah is near” [al-Baqarah 2:214]. And He said, relating that Yaʿqūb told his sons:
“My sons, go and seek news of Yūsuf and his brother, and do not despair of the relief of Allah” [Yūsuf 12:87]; and then He told the story of their reunion straight after that.

How many stories has He, Glorified is He, told of relieving the distress of His prophets when the distress was at its height: saving Nūḥ and those with him in the Ark, saving Ibrāhīm from the fire, ransoming his son whom he had been commanded to sacrifice, saving Mūsā and his people from the sea

and drowning their enemy, the story of Ayyūb and of Yūnus, and the stories of Muḥammad ﷺ with his enemies and his deliverance from them, such as his story in the cave, and on the days of Badr, Uḥud, the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), Ḥunayn and others.

His words ﷺ, “And with hardship comes ease,” are drawn from the words of the Exalted, “Allah will bring ease after hardship” [al-Ṭalāq 65:7], and His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: “For indeed, with hardship comes ease; indeed, with hardship comes ease” [al-Sharḥ 94:5–6].
Al-Bazzār recorded in his Musnad, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim — the wording being his — from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“If hardship came and entered this hole, ease would come and enter after it and drive it out.” And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: “For indeed, with hardship comes ease; indeed, with hardship comes ease.”
Ibn Jarīr and others narrated something similar from the hadith of al-Ḥasan in mursal form, and in his hadith the Prophet ﷺ said: “One hardship will never overcome two eases.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated with his chain from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: If hardship entered a hole, ease would come and enter with it. Then he said: Allah the Exalted said: “For indeed, with hardship comes ease; indeed, with hardship comes ease.”

With his chain, too, he narrated that Abū ʿUbaydah was besieged, and ʿUmar wrote to him, saying: Whatever hardship befalls a man, Allah will bring relief after it; one hardship will never overcome two eases. And He says:
“Be patient, outdo [your enemies] in patience, stand guard, and fear Allah, that you may succeed” [Āl ʿImrān 3:200].

Among the subtle secrets of relief being joined to distress, and ease to hardship, is that when distress grows severe, becomes great and reaches its limit, the servant despairs of its being lifted by any created being, and his heart attaches itself to Allah alone.

This is the reality of reliance on Allah (tawakkul), and it is one of the greatest means by which needs are sought; for Allah suffices whoever relies on Him, as the Exalted said: “And whoever relies on Allah, He is sufficient for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:3].
Ādam ibn Abī Iyās narrated in his Tafsīr, with his chain, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: Mālik al-Ashjaʿī came to the Prophet ﷺ
and said: My son ʿAwf has been taken captive. He said to him: Send word to him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commands you to say often:

There is no might and no power except through Allah. The messenger came and told him, and ʿAwf set about saying: There is no might and no power except through Allah. They had bound him with rawhide thongs, and the thongs fell off him.

He went out and came upon a she-camel of theirs, and rode it. As he came along, he came upon the grazing herd of the people who had bound him, and he called out to them, and the last of them followed the first.

His parents had no warning until he was calling at the door. His father said: ʿAwf, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah! His mother said: Alas — while ʿAwf lies miserable, suffering from the thongs he is bound with!

The father and the servant raced to him, and there was ʿAwf, who had filled the courtyard with camels. He told his father what had happened to him and to the camels, and his father went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ
and told him the news of ʿAwf and of the camels. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: “Do with them as you like, as you would do with your own camels.”

And there was revealed: “And whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect; and whoever relies on Allah, He is sufficient for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:2–3], to the end of the verse.
Al-Fuḍayl said: By Allah, if you despaired of creation so completely that you wanted nothing from them, your Master would give you everything you want.

Ibrāhīm ibn Adham mentioned that someone said: Those who ask have never asked with anything more importunate than the servant's saying, “Whatever Allah wills” (mā shāʾ Allāh). He said: By that he meant entrusting one's affairs wholly to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
The printed text reads ألحلف, an evident misprint; read ألحف (“more importunate”), as in other editions of the book.
Saʿīd ibn Sālim al-Qaddāḥ said: It has reached me that Mūsā (peace be upon him) had a need from Allah. He sought it, and it was slow in coming, so he said: Whatever Allah wills.
And there was his need, before him. He was amazed, and Allah revealed to him: Did you not know that your saying “Whatever Allah wills” is the most successful means by which needs are sought?
Moreover, when the believer finds relief slow in coming and despairs of it after much supplication and humble entreaty, with no sign of an answer appearing, he turns on himself with blame,
saying to it: It is only because of you that this has come upon me; had there been any good in you, I would have been answered. This blame is more beloved to Allah than many acts of obedience,

for it brings about the servant's brokenness before his Master and his admission that he deserves the affliction that has come upon him and does not deserve to have his supplication answered. That is why the answer to his supplication and the relief of his distress then come to him swiftly, for the Exalted is with those whose hearts are broken for His sake.

Wahb said: A man worshipped for a long time, and then he had a need from Allah. He fasted seventy weeks, eating eleven dates each week, then asked Allah for his need, and it was not granted. He turned on himself and said:

It is because of you that this has come upon me. Had there been any good in you, your need would have been granted. At that, an angel came down to him and said: Son of Ādam, this hour of yours is better than all your past worship, and Allah has fulfilled your need.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
One of the early poets has verses on this theme:
Perhaps what you see will not last, and you will see / relief from what fate has pressed upon you.
Perhaps relief will come, brought by Allah, for He / has, every day, some new affair among His creation.
When hardship appears, hope for ease, for / Allah has decreed that ease follows hardship.
